Государственный стандарт по русскому языку как иностранному. Базовый уровень (2-е изд., «Златоуст», 2001; full text read directly from https://test.irlc.msu.ru/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/A2_standart.pdf)

Государственный образовательный стандарт по русскому языку как иностранному. Первый уровень. Общее владение («Златоуст», 1999; full text read directly from https://kpfu.ru/portal/docs/F_189607702/Gosudarstvennyj.standart.Uroven.1.pdf)

Государственный образовательный стандарт по русскому языку как иностранному. Второй уровень. Общее владение («Златоуст», 1999; full text read directly from https://test.irlc.msu.ru/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/B2_standart.pdf)

Государственный образовательный стандарт по русскому языку как иностранному. Третий уровень. Общее владение («Златоуст», 1999; full text read directly from a copy of https://test.tsu.ru/sites/default/files/files/exams/C1_standart.pdf) — sections 2.2.3 through 2.2.8 (adjective, pronoun, verb, numeral, adverb, function words) did not extract from this copy and were not used; see report.

a1.name: Noun gender and number
a1.note: Every Russian noun has one of three genders and a singular/plural number, and this shows up on any adjective or past-tense verb that agrees with it, not on the noun's own ending alone.
a1.test: The sentence has a noun whose gender or number is visible on an agreeing adjective, possessive, or past-tense verb.

a1.name: Nominative case
a1.note: The nominative names the subject of a sentence, a person being addressed, or what something is called; it is the dictionary form.
a1.test: A nominative noun functions as the sentence's subject, a direct address, or a bare naming of a person/thing.

a1.name: Zero copula in the present tense
a1.note: Russian has no present-tense verb 'to be': a noun or adjective predicate stands directly after its subject, often separated by a dash in writing.
a1.test: A present-time sentence links a subject to a noun or adjective predicate with no verb between them.

a1.name: Genitive: possession and absence
a1.note: The genitive without a preposition marks whose something is, and, with нет, marks that something is absent (in the present tense at this level); it also follows 2, 3, 4 and the number in a date.
a1.test: A genitive noun follows another noun to show possession, follows нет to show absence, or follows a number 2–4 or a date.

a1.name: Genitive: source of motion and possessor with у
a1.note: Из and с plus the genitive name where a movement started; у plus the genitive names who owns something in a У + genitive + есть sentence.
a1.example: Мы пришли с концерта. У Андрея есть машина.
a1.test: A genitive noun follows из or с naming a starting point, or follows у naming a possessor in an есть-sentence.

a1.name: Dative: addressee and age
a1.note: The dative without a preposition marks who receives an action, and, with a personal pronoun, whose age is being stated.
a1.test: A dative noun/pronoun names who an action is directed at, or appears in an age sentence (dative + number + лет/год).

a1.name: Dative with к: goal of motion
a1.note: К plus the dative names the person someone is heading toward.
a1.test: A dative noun follows к and names the person that motion is directed toward.

a1.name: Accusative: direct object, звать, and duration
a1.note: The accusative without a preposition marks the direct object of a transitive verb, the person named in a Х зовут construction, and how long something lasted.
a1.example: Андрей купил журнал. Меня зовут Лена.
a1.test: An accusative noun/pronoun is a verb's direct object, or is the logical subject of зовут, or states a duration.

a1.name: Animacy in the accusative
a1.note: A masculine noun naming a person or animal takes an accusative form identical to its genitive, not its nominative; this does not happen with feminine or neuter nouns or with things.
a1.test: A masculine singular noun naming a person/animal is a direct object and its ending matches its genitive rather than its nominative.

a1.name: Accusative with в/на: direction and clock time
a1.note: В and на plus the accusative name the destination of motion, and в plus the accusative names an hour or a day of the week.
a1.example: Утром я иду в институт. В среду была экскурсия.
a1.test: An accusative noun follows в or на naming a destination, or follows в naming an hour or a weekday.

a1.name: Instrumental without a preposition: заниматься and profession
a1.note: The instrumental without a preposition follows заниматься/увлекаться-type verbs, and names a profession after быть.
a1.test: An instrumental noun follows заниматься/увлекаться, or names a profession after быть.

a1.name: Instrumental with с: accompaniment
a1.note: С plus the instrumental names who or what accompanies something.
a1.test: An instrumental noun follows с and names something that accompanies another thing.

a1.name: Prepositional case: topic, place, and vehicle
a1.note: The prepositional case, which only ever appears with a preposition, marks the topic of speech or thought after о, location after в/на, and the vehicle used after на.
a1.example: Мы были в театре. Я думаю о семье.
a1.test: A prepositional-case noun follows о naming a topic, or follows в/на naming a place or a vehicle.

a1.name: Personal pronouns in oblique cases
a1.note: Personal pronouns (я, ты, он, она, мы, вы, они) change form completely outside the nominative and must match the case their position requires.
a1.test: A personal pronoun appears in a non-nominative form (меня, тебе, его, ей, нас, etc.) matching what its case requires.

a1.name: Question, possessive, demonstrative, and negative pronouns
a1.note: Какой/чей/сколько ask about a noun's properties, мой/твой mark possession, этот points something out, and никто/ничто negate.
a1.test: The sentence uses a question, possessive, demonstrative, or negative pronoun agreeing with its noun where relevant.

a1.name: Full adjective agreement
a1.note: A full adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number, and, in the nominative, in case as well.
a1.test: A full adjective directly modifies a noun and its ending matches that noun's gender and number.

a1.name: Short adjectives: рад, занят, должен, болен
a1.note: This small closed set of adjectives is used only in its short predicate form, agreeing with the subject in gender and number, never as a modifier before a noun.
a1.test: рад/занят/должен/болен appears as the predicate, agreeing in gender/number with its subject.

a1.name: Verbal aspect: imperfective vs. perfective
a1.note: Most Russian verbs come in pairs: the imperfective names an ongoing or repeated action, the perfective names one completed event. Choosing the wrong member of the pair changes what the sentence means, not just its style.
a1.example: Вчера я читал книгу весь вечер. Вчера я прочитал книгу.
a1.test: The verb's aspect (imperfective for process/repetition, perfective for a single completed event) matches what the sentence describes.

a1.name: Present, past, and future tense
a1.note: Present tense exists only for imperfective verbs; the future is буду + imperfective infinitive for an ongoing future action, or the simple present-tense-looking form of a perfective verb for a single future event.
a1.test: A finite verb is correctly marked for present, past, or future, and its future form matches its aspect (буду+infinitive for imperfective, simple form for perfective).

a1.name: First and second conjugation
a1.note: Present/future verb endings fall into two conjugation patterns, plus a handful of individually memorized irregular verbs.
a1.test: A present/future-tense verb form matches the ending pattern of its conjugation class.

a1.name: Imperative
a1.note: The imperative addresses ты or вы directly and has its own ending, distinct from the present tense.
a1.test: The sentence contains an imperative verb form directed at ты or вы.

a1.name: Verb government and transitivity
a1.note: Each verb fixes the case (or preposition) of the noun that follows it; a transitive verb takes a plain accusative object, while its intransitive counterpart, if any, needs a preposition instead.
a1.example: Я встретил брата. Я встретился с братом.
a1.test: A verb is followed by exactly the case or preposition it is known to govern.

a1.name: Verbs of motion: идти/ходить and ехать/ездить
a1.note: Unprefixed motion verbs split into a one-directional member for a single trip now under way and a multidirectional member for habitual, repeated, or round trips.
a1.example: Я иду в магазин. Я хожу в бассейн по средам.
a1.test: идти/ехать is used for one trip currently happening in one direction, or ходить/ездить is used for a repeated or round trip.

a1.name: Motion verbs with по- and при-
a1.note: По- added to a motion verb marks setting off; при- marks arriving.
a1.example: Он пошёл домой. Она пришла в шесть.
a1.test: A motion verb carries по- with a setting-off meaning or при- with an arrival meaning.

a1.name: Numerals один–пять and the noun's case
a1.note: The noun after один stays nominative singular, after два/три/четыре it takes genitive singular, and after пять and up it takes genitive plural.
a1.example: У меня два брата. Билет стоит пять рублей.
a1.test: A cardinal numeral is followed by a noun in the case its value requires (nominative/genitive singular/genitive plural).

a1.name: Ordinal numerals
a1.note: Ordinal numerals agree with their noun like adjectives and are used for dates and rank.
a1.test: An ordinal numeral agrees with its noun in gender/number/case, often in a date.

a1.name: Adverbs and можно/нужно/нельзя
a1.note: Adverbs of place, time, manner, and degree modify verbs or adjectives; можно/нужно/нельзя combine with an infinitive to express permission, necessity, or prohibition, with no subject required.
a1.test: An adverb modifies a verb/adjective, or можно/нужно/нельзя is followed by an infinitive.

a1.name: Statement, question, and command sentences
a1.note: A sentence is marked as a statement, a question, or a command by its word order, question word, or verb form, independent of the words used.
a1.test: The sentence is clearly a statement, a question, or a command by its structure and punctuation.

a1.name: Compound sentences with и, а, но, или
a1.note: Two independent clauses are joined by one of these coordinating conjunctions to add, contrast, or offer an alternative.
a1.example: Я читаю, а брат смотрит телевизор.
a1.test: Two independent clauses are joined by и, а, но, or или.

a1.name: Subordinate clauses with что, чтобы, когда, потому что
a1.note: A main clause takes a subordinate clause that reports content (что/чтобы), gives a time (когда), or gives a reason (потому что).
a1.test: A main clause is followed by a subordinate clause introduced by что, чтобы, когда, or потому что.

a1.name: Neutral word order
a1.note: In a plain statement the subject precedes the predicate, a modifying adjective precedes its noun, and a place/time phrase that opens the sentence is followed first by the predicate, then the subject.
a1.test: The sentence follows this neutral ordering rather than an unusual or emphatic one.

a2.name: Genitive: absence in the past, part of a whole, and a full date
a2.note: Absence with нет now also covers the past tense (не было), the genitive marks a part taken from a whole, много/мало/несколько take a genitive noun, and a full date adds the year.
a2.example: В городе не было театра. Выпейте чашку чая.
a2.test: A genitive noun marks past-tense absence with не было, a part of a whole, a quantity after много/мало/несколько, or a year in a full date.

a2.name: Genitive with от, до, у, and time prepositions
a2.note: От and до mark the start and end of a route; у marks being at someone's place; после/во время/до mark when something happened relative to another event.
a2.example: Я был у врача. Как доехать до парка?
a2.test: A genitive noun follows от/до marking a route's endpoints, у marking whose place someone is at, or после/во время/до marking relative time.

a2.name: Dative experiencer with a nominative stimulus
a2.note: Verbs like нравиться and impersonal states put the person who feels something in the dative while the thing felt or liked stands in the nominative as the grammatical subject; this also covers age for any noun, not only pronouns.
a2.example: Андрею нравится футбол. Моему другу двадцать лет.
a2.test: A dative noun/pronoun names an experiencer while a nominative noun is the grammatical subject of the liking/state verb, or a dative noun states an age.

a2.name: Dative with по: route, medium, and subject label
a2.note: По plus the dative names the surface someone moves along, the medium something is seen/heard through, and, before a subject name, what a book or lesson is about.
a2.example: Я иду по улице. Это учебник по математике.
a2.test: A dative noun follows по in the sense of a route, a medium (radio/TV), or a subject label.

a2.name: Instrumental with над/под/рядом с
a2.note: These prepositions plus the instrumental locate something above, below, or next to a landmark.
a2.test: An instrumental noun follows над, под, or рядом с and locates something relative to it.

a2.name: Prepositional case for time
a2.note: В plus a month, and на plus an ordinal-marked week, place a point in time in the prepositional case, extending the case beyond its A1 uses of topic/place/vehicle.
a2.example: Друг приехал в сентябре, на прошлой неделе.
a2.test: A prepositional-case noun follows в or на naming when something happened.

a2.name: Animacy in the accusative: plural of every gender
a2.note: The rule that an animate direct object copies the genitive rather than the nominative now applies to plural nouns regardless of gender, not only to masculine singular ones.
a2.test: A plural noun naming people/animals is a direct object and its ending matches the genitive plural.

a2.name: Adjective declension through all cases
a2.note: A full adjective now changes for every case its noun takes, not just the nominative it was limited to at the previous level.
a2.test: A full adjective agrees with its noun in a non-nominative case.

a2.name: Irregular comparative adjectives
a2.note: A handful of common adjectives form their comparative irregularly rather than with a regular suffix.
a2.test: An adjective appears in one of its irregular comparative forms (лучше, хуже, больше, меньше).

a2.name: Wider noun and adjective word-formation suffixes
a2.note: New productive suffixes build agent nouns (-чик/-щик and more), abstract nouns (-ство, -ость, -ация), and adjectives (-ов-, -еньк-).
a2.test: The sentence contains a noun or adjective built from a known root with one of these newly taught suffixes.

a2.name: Motion verbs: more base pairs and more prefixes
a2.note: У-, вы-, and в- join по-/при- as directional prefixes, and лететь/летать, нести/носить, and везти/возить join идти/ходить and ехать/ездить as base motion-verb pairs.
a2.example: Он вышел из дома. Она принесла цветы.
a2.test: A motion verb from one of the five base pairs carries one of по-/при-/у-/вы-/в- with the matching direction.

a2.name: Word order and information structure
a2.note: Moving a phrase to the front of the sentence shifts what question the sentence is understood to answer, because Russian marks new information by position rather than by stress alone.
a2.test: The sentence's word order departs from the plain subject-first order to foreground a particular piece of information.

a2.name: Subordinate clauses with который, если, чтобы
a2.note: Relative clauses with который, conditional clauses with если, and purpose clauses with чтобы widen the range of subordination available.
a2.example: Если у меня будет время, я приду.
a2.test: The sentence has a subordinate clause introduced by который, если, or чтобы.

a2.name: Reported speech
a2.note: A question or statement is folded into a reported clause with что or a question word, dropping the quotation marks and adjusting pronouns.
a2.example: Он спросил, где Петя. Я сказал, что Петя в театре.
a2.test: A verb of saying/asking is followed by a reported clause introduced by что or a question word, without direct quotation.

b1.name: Genitive as verb object and standard of comparison
b1.note: Certain verbs like желать take a genitive object rather than an accusative one, and a comparative adjective's standard of comparison, when expressed without чем, stands in the genitive.
b1.example: Желаю вам счастья. Самолёт быстрее поезда.
b1.test: A genitive noun is the object of a verb like желать, or is the unmarked standard after a comparative adjective.

b1.name: Genitive with a wider set of location prepositions
b1.note: Около, вокруг, (не)далеко от, справа от, and слева от all govern the genitive to place something relative to a landmark.
b1.test: A genitive noun follows около/вокруг/(не)далеко от/справа от/слева от.

b1.name: Instrumental: means and the passive agent
b1.note: The instrumental without a preposition can name the tool or means used for an action, or, together with a passive participle, the person who performed it.
b1.test: An instrumental noun names either the instrument of an action or, with a passive participle, its agent.

b1.name: Instrumental with перед and descriptive с
b1.note: Перед plus the instrumental gives a point in time just before an event; с plus the instrumental after a noun describes a feature that helps identify it.
b1.example: Перед экзаменом я всегда волнуюсь. Дом с большими окнами.
b1.test: An instrumental noun follows перед marking time-before, or follows a noun + с marking a defining feature.

b1.name: Reflexive pronoun себя
b1.note: Себя has no nominative form and always refers back to the subject of its own clause, whoever that subject is.
b1.test: себя/себе/собой refers back to the subject of the clause it stands in.

b1.name: Regular comparative and superlative adjectives
b1.note: Beyond the irregular forms learned earlier, adjectives now form a regular comparative and a superlative, analytically or with a suffix.
b1.test: An adjective appears in a regularly formed comparative or superlative.

b1.name: Comparative adverbs
b1.note: Adverbs, like adjectives, form a comparative degree of their own.
b1.test: An adverb appears in its comparative form.

b1.name: Numeral + adjective + noun agreement
b1.note: When an adjective comes between a numeral and its noun, the adjective's case and number follow the same rule that governs the noun after that numeral.
b1.test: A numeral, an adjective, and a noun combine, and the adjective's form follows the numeral's agreement rule.

b1.name: Reflexive -ся verbs (non-passive)
b1.note: Some verbs add -ся to mean an action turned back on the subject or shared between subjects, with no passive sense at all.
b1.test: A -ся verb is used reflexively or reciprocally, not to mark a passive.

b1.name: Passive voice
b1.note: A short passive participle, or a -ся verb used passively, promotes the action's target to the grammatical subject.
b1.example: План составлен Игорем. Дом строится рабочими.
b1.test: The sentence has a short passive participle or a passive -ся verb, with the logical object as its nominative subject.

b1.name: Predicate noun in the instrumental after стать/быть in the future
b1.note: A predicate noun after стать, or after быть in the future tense, stands in the instrumental rather than the nominative.
b1.test: A predicate noun after станет/будет/стать is in the instrumental case.

b1.name: Short adjective + infinitive
b1.note: A predicative short adjective can take an infinitive to express what the subject is glad, ready, or obliged to do.
b1.test: A short adjective (рад, готов, должен, etc.) is followed by an infinitive it governs.

b1.name: Participles (причастие)
b1.note: A participle is an adjective built from a verb, active or passive, and it agrees with its noun exactly as any adjective does.
b1.test: The sentence contains a participle (an -щий/-вший/-нный/-тый-type form) agreeing with the noun it modifies.

b1.name: Short-form passive participle
b1.note: The short passive participle drops the long ending and agrees only in gender and number, functioning as a predicate rather than a modifier.
b1.test: A short passive participle (-н/-на/-но/-ны or -т/-та/-то/-ты) is used as the sentence's predicate.

b1.name: Gerunds (деепричастие)
b1.note: A gerund is an unchanging verb form describing an action carried out by the same subject alongside the main action.
b1.test: The sentence contains a gerund (-я/-а for imperfective, -в/-вши for perfective) whose implied subject is the main clause's subject.

b1.name: Motion verbs with пере-, про-, о-, за-, до-, от-
b1.note: These prefixes add crossing, passing, going around, starting to go, reaching a point, and moving away as distinct spatial meanings to the motion-verb system.
b1.example: Мы перешли улицу. Он дошёл до вокзала.
b1.test: A motion verb carries one of пере-/про-/о-/за-/до-/от- with its matching spatial meaning.

b1.name: Concessive and degree clauses
b1.note: Хотя and несмотря на то что introduce a fact that doesn't stop the main clause from being true; чем...тем links two things that grow or shrink together.
b1.example: Хотя было холодно, мы пошли гулять.
b1.test: The sentence has a хотя/несмотря на то что concessive clause, or a чем...тем correlative pair.

b1.name: Clauses of cause (так как) and manner (как)
b1.note: Так как gives a reason, placed either before or after the result it explains; как introduces how something is or was done.
b1.example: Так как шёл дождь, мы остались дома.
b1.test: The sentence contains a так как causal clause or a как-clause of manner.

b2.name: Genitive as the object of deverbal nouns and ждать-type verbs
b2.note: A noun built from a verb, and a small class of verbs like ждать, take a genitive object or a genitive 'subject' rather than an accusative one.
b2.example: Я жду помощи от вас. Замечания коллег мне интересны.
b2.test: A genitive noun is the object of a ждать-type verb or of a deverbal noun, or is the logical subject of a deverbal noun.

b2.name: Genitive with от for purpose and cause
b2.note: От plus the genitive names what a remedy is for, or, with из/от/из-за, the emotional or external cause of something.
b2.example: Надо купить лекарство от гриппа. Мы не гуляли из-за дождя.
b2.test: A genitive noun follows от naming what something counters, or follows из/от/из-за naming a cause.

b2.name: Dative as the logical subject of an impersonal predicate
b2.note: An infinitive-based impersonal predicate (necessity, possibility, or its negation) puts the person concerned in the dative rather than the nominative.
b2.example: Тане надо спросить друзей об этом. Автобусу здесь не проехать.
b2.test: A dative noun/pronoun is the logical subject of an infinitive-based impersonal predicate.

b2.name: Dative with по for a recurring day
b2.note: По plus a plural dative day name marks when something happens on a regular basis.
b2.test: A dative noun follows по and names a day/time that recurs regularly.

b2.name: Accusative experiencer with no nominative subject
b2.note: A closed set of verbs describing a bodily or emotional state take their experiencer in the accusative and have no nominative subject at all.
b2.test: An accusative noun/pronoun is the sole argument of a subjectless verb of bodily or emotional state.

b2.name: Accusative with за, на, and через for time
b2.note: За marks how long a completed action took, на marks how long something is borrowed or planned for, and через marks how soon something will happen.
b2.example: Я выучил язык за год. Соревнования будут через месяц.
b2.test: An accusative noun follows за, на, or через in one of these three time senses.

b2.name: Instrumental as the object of руководить/восхищаться, and manner/time
b2.note: A closed set of verbs like руководить and восхищаться take a plain instrumental object, and the instrumental alone can also mark the manner of an action or a recurring time of day.
b2.example: Профессор руководит кафедрой. Вечерами я люблю читать.
b2.test: An instrumental noun is the object of a verb that specifically governs it, or names manner or a recurring time of day.

b2.name: Instrumental with с for a co-participant and manner
b2.note: С plus the instrumental names someone who did something together with the subject, or describes how something was said or done.
b2.example: Мы с руководителем обсудили результаты. Он говорил с улыбкой.
b2.test: An instrumental noun follows с naming who acted together with the subject, or describing manner.

b2.name: Aspect choice in the imperative, negation, and conditional
b2.note: Perfective and imperfective carry different nuances outside the indicative too: a perfective imperative is a one-off instruction, an imperfective one a standing rule; a negated verb's aspect shifts between forbidding an event and warning against a habit.
b2.example: Не забудь позвонить! Не звони поздно вечером.
b2.test: An imperative or a negated verb uses the aspect appropriate to its nuance (single event vs. general rule/habit).

b2.name: Conditional/subjunctive mood with бы
b2.note: A past-tense verb form plus бы expresses a wish, a polite request, or a hypothetical condition, detached from any real time reference.
b2.example: Я бы хотел поехать в Москву. Если бы у меня было время, я бы пришёл.
b2.test: The sentence has a past-tense verb followed by бы, expressing a wish, politeness, or a hypothetical.

b2.name: Full active and passive participle phrases
b2.note: A long participle, active or passive, can carry its own dependents and head a phrase that modifies a noun much like a relative clause.
b2.example: Студент, читающий газету, живёт рядом. Прочитанная всеми книга стала бестселлером.
b2.test: A long participle heads a phrase (with its own dependents) modifying a noun.

b2.name: Gerund phrases
b2.note: A gerund can take its own object or adverbial, forming a full phrase that explains when, how, or why the main action happens.
b2.example: Изучая теорию, надо помнить о практике.
b2.test: A gerund heads a phrase with its own dependent, attached to the main clause.

b2.name: Lexical verb prefixes beyond motion
b2.note: The same prefixes used on motion verbs also attach to ordinary verbs to change their meaning outright — finishing, redoing, writing down — not just their aspect or direction.
b2.example: Я дописал письмо. Она переписала текст.
b2.test: A verb carries a prefix (в-, вы-, за-, до-, из-, на-, о-, от-, пере-, при-, про-, под-, раз-, с-, у-) that changes its base meaning, on a non-motion verb.

b2.name: Finer temporal subordinators
b2.note: Пока, пока не, после того как, до того как, прежде чем, and по мере того как sequence or overlap two events more precisely than когда alone.
b2.example: Позвони мне, прежде чем идти. Подожди, пока я не вернусь.
b2.test: The sentence has a subordinate clause introduced by пока, пока не, после того как, до того как, прежде чем, or по мере того как.

b2.name: Nominalized predicate in formal register
b2.note: In an official or news-style register, a plain verb is often replaced by a light verb plus a noun built from it, which is how formal Russian tends to phrase an action.
b2.example: Президент прибыл с визитом в Африку.
b2.test: The sentence's predicate is a light verb plus a deverbal or descriptive noun phrase, in place of a single plain verb, in a formal register.

c1.name: Genitive with из/от/для for material, origin, and purpose
c1.note: Из names what something is made of, от names where it came from, and для names who or what it is intended for.
c1.example: Костюм из шерсти очень красив. Мне надо купить альбом для рисунков.
c1.test: A genitive noun follows из, от, or для in a material, origin, or purpose sense.

c1.name: Genitive experiencer and emotional cause
c1.note: У plus the genitive names who feels a bodily sensation, and со/от plus the genitive names the emotion behind a reaction.
c1.example: У мальчика колет в боку. Я бы умер со стыда.
c1.test: A genitive noun follows у naming who feels a bodily sensation, or follows со/от naming an emotional cause.

c1.name: Genitive with мимо, вдоль, напротив, из-за, из-под
c1.note: This wider set of place prepositions, alongside накануне/до/после/с...до.../около for time, all govern the genitive.
c1.example: Автобус идёт мимо музея. Из-под стола вылез котёнок.
c1.test: A genitive noun follows мимо, вдоль, напротив, из-за, или из-под, or one of the finer time prepositions (накануне, с...до..., около).

c1.name: Dative object of мешать/радоваться/принадлежать-type verbs
c1.note: A further set of verbs — hindering, rejoicing at, belonging to — governs a plain dative object.
c1.example: Ты мешаешь брату заниматься. Леса в стране принадлежат государству.
c1.test: A dative noun is the object of a verb from this set (мешать, радоваться, принадлежать, and similar).

c1.name: Accusative for time-filled, approximate amount, goal, and topic
c1.note: The accusative marks how much of a period an action filled, an approximate quantity with с, a goal with за, and a topic with про.
c1.example: Мы разговаривали всю дорогу. Надо бороться за счастье.
c1.test: An accusative noun expresses the extent of a time period, an approximate quantity after с, a goal after за, or a topic after про.

c1.name: Instrumental with считаться/обладать/следить за and similar
c1.note: A further set of verbs — being regarded as, possessing, keeping track of, competing with — governs the instrumental, with or without a preposition.
c1.example: Писатель отличается знанием современной жизни. Я слежу за событиями в мире.
c1.test: An instrumental noun (with or without a preposition) is governed by считаться, обладать, отличаться, следить за, соревноваться с, or a similar verb.

c1.name: Instrumental with с naming a defining feature
c1.note: С plus the instrumental, right after a noun, names a feature that helps identify or describe it.
c1.example: На площади стоит дом с колоннами.
c1.test: A noun is followed by с + instrumental naming a physical or personal feature that identifies it.

c1.name: Prepositional with при for condition, and for appearance
c1.note: При plus the prepositional gives the circumstance under which something happens, and the prepositional also names a garment or feature that identifies a person.
c1.example: При свете луны читать трудно. Девушка в светлом платье вбежала в комнату.
c1.test: A prepositional-case noun follows при naming a circumstance, or names a garment/feature identifying a person.

c1.name: Inversion for emphasis
c1.note: Word order can deliberately depart from the neutral subject-first pattern to give a word rhetorical weight, while staying fully grammatical.
c1.example: Тревога есть тревога, сигнал есть сигнал.
c1.test: The sentence's word order departs from the neutral pattern for emphasis, and remains grammatical.

c1.name: Prefixed reflexive verbs with a resultative meaning
c1.note: A directional or completive prefix combined with -ся forms a verb whose meaning is neither the plain prefixed verb nor a simple reflexive, but its own resultative sense.
c1.example: Ребёнок наигрался и заснул. Мы договорились встретиться завтра.
c1.test: A verb combines a prefix with -ся carrying the resultative/completive meaning specific to that combination, not a literal reflexive or passive reading.

c1.name: Substantivized adjectives
c1.note: An adjective can function as the noun of its phrase in its own right, while still declining exactly like an adjective.
c1.test: An adjective-form word is the head noun of its phrase (no noun follows it) and declines as an adjective would.
